stem: You plan an iterative workload that uses Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), where a learned noise model should stay valid across many jobs. Why is a session particularly suited to this, compared with batch or job mode?

options.text: Sessions automatically re-learn the noise model before every single job of an iterative workload, so PEC always uses fresh calibration data; batch cannot.
Only sessions support error mitigation; batch and job mode typically disable PEC entirely.
In a dedicated session the jobs run close together, so a noise model learned once stays valid for the jobs that follow.
PEC requires exclusive access because it physically recalibrates the QPU hardware between jobs.
A session lets the Estimator cache the learned noise model inside the primitive object, which batch and job mode typically discard between jobs.
PEC learning runs as a separate calibration job that a session is allowed to submit, so batch and job mode fall back to ZNE.

explanation.correct: A session's dedicated window keeps jobs running tightly together, so you can learn the noise model once and reuse it while it is still accurate. In batch or job mode a later job can spend so long in the queue that the device drifts and the learned model becomes stale.

distractors.A: The advantage is learning the model ONCE and reusing it while it is still accurate, not re-learning it before every job.
distractors.B: Error mitigation options are available in all execution modes; the mode affects scheduling and how long a learned model stays valid, not whether mitigation is allowed.
distractors.D: PEC is a software post-processing technique; it does not recalibrate hardware. The benefit of a session is timing, not physical recalibration.
distractors.E: Nothing is cached client-side in the primitive: a fresh `EstimatorV2` in a session learns exactly as much as one in a batch. What a session buys is elapsed time — the model stays representative because the device has not drifted.
distractors.F: Learning is part of the primitive's own execution, not a privileged calibration job, and no mode silently swaps your mitigation technique for another one. PEC is available outside sessions; it is only less economical there.
